title: Where does your blood go
on a hard effort?
aim: As exercise gets longer or harder, blood is redirected from the gut to the working muscles; carbohydrate advice during exercise depends on how long you go.
takeaways: During exercise, blood flow is redistributed from the gut to the working muscles.
With prolonged and/or intense exercise, gut blood flow may fall by 80% or more.
Carbohydrate advice during exercise scales with duration, from a mouth rinse in about an hour to about 90 g/h in ultra-endurance events.
unknowns: No data link g/h to heart-rate zones or gut blood flow.
refs: Threshold for significant GI perturbations (≥2 h at 60% VO2max)
Splanchnic blood flow ↓ ≥80% with prolonged and/or intense exercise; redistribution to working muscles
Carbohydrate intake during exercise by duration (mouth rinse ~1 h; ~60 g/h 2–3 h; ~90 g/h ultra, multiple transportable carbohydrates)

claims.quote: With prolonged duration and/or intensity, the SBF may be decreased by 80% or more.
during exercise lasting approximately 1 h in duration, a mouth rinse or small amounts of carbohydrate can result in a performance benefit
A single carbohydrate source can be oxidized at rates up to approximately 60 g/h and this is the recommendation for exercise that is more prolonged (2-3 h).
For ultra-endurance events, the recommendation is higher at approximately 90 g/h.
Exercise stress of ≥2 hours at 60% VO2max appears to be the threshold whereby significant gastrointestinal perturbations manifest, irrespective of fitness status.
claims.note: PubMed record reads "60% VO" (subscript lost). Check spelling in the full text before publishing.
